Fire is a regular occurrence on the Swan Coastal Plain, including low-moderate severity prescribed burning for risk reduction and conservation purposes during autumn and spring periods, and high severity wildfires mostly from human-caused ignitions during the hot, dry summer period (Densmore and Clingan 2019; Enright and Fontaine 2014; Howard et al. 2020; Plucinski 2014). The proximity of urban and peri-urban Banksia woodlands to human homes and infrastructure has placed substantial attention and importance on fire management in this ecosystem. While there are no direct estimates of historical or long-term fire intervals in Banksia woodlands that might suggest lower or upper limits to their adaptations, they share attributes (e.g., key plant functional types, surface and elevated fuel types) with surrounding vegetation types, including shrublands to the north and eucalypt forests to the east and south, where typical fire intervals have been estimated at 10–40+ years (shrublands) and 5–20 years (low severity, forest) or 20–100 years (high severity, forest) (Burrows, Ward, and Robinson 1995; Enright et al. 2012; Enright and Thomas 2008; Murphy et al. 2013). Indigenous use of fire was widespread in the region prior to European colonisation but specific information regarding burning in Banksia woodlands is not clear (Lullfitz et al. 2020; Rodrigues et al. 2022).

#### **2.2 | Study Species**

To explore fire interval effects on reproduction, we chose six woody plant species with a range of growth forms, fire response traits and seed bank storage modes across four common plant families (Table 1). All species are native, common and widespread in Banksia woodlands and considered indicators of the vegetation type; although varying in their abundance and distribution within the landscape (Gibson et al. 1994). Serotinous (canopy seed bank) species typically accumulate woody fruits containing seeds (hereafter cones) in the canopy over multiple years, therefore allowing assessment of cumulative reproductive output. In the study area, the two selected *Banksia* species are known to be weakly serotinous, with most seeds released from woody fruits (hereafter cones) within 1–2 years of cone maturity (Cowling and Lamont 1985). The dioecious shrub species *Allocasuarina humilis* is moderately serotinous with female plants retaining seeds in cones for up to 5 years (personal obs.). By pairing serotinous species with species with other seed storage modes, here specifically soil seed banks, we aim to gain an insight into the response of the broader plant community.

#### **2.3 | Site Selection**

To assess varying fire intervals, we employed a space-for-time approach and selected sites with a broad range of recent fire histories (time since fire, TSF). We first interrogated fire history data for remnant vegetation in urban and peri-urban reserves across the study region to identify a set of candidate sites with a wide range of fire ages, suitable access (with permission from land managers) and appropriate vegetation type (i.e., not wetland, riparian, or limestone vegetation). Year of last fire for each site was determined from spatial data layers maintained by the Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA-060, https://catalogue.data.wa.gov.au/dataset/dbca-fire-history); historical satellite and aerial imagery (Landgate, https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html); and local government records. Given limitations in fire history records and satellite and aerial imagery, we were unable to confirm exact ages for some sites beyond 35 years (occurring before approximately 1986). Sites with no assignable post-fire age are referred to here as long unburnt (LUB), and for analysis are given a notional age of 35 years.

We visited candidate sites to confirm the above criteria as well as the presence of the study species and the absence of

This produced a total of 34 sites across a fire interval chronosequence from 1 to 35 years (or more), with each site containing one to five study species. The number of sites surveyed for each species ranged from 11 to 17, all spanning a similar post-fire chronosequence (Table 1). Some sites were surveyed over two successive years, creating two nonindependent TSF samples.

Sites were mostly (91%) located on Spearwood sands across a 100 km north–south extent of the Swan Coastal Plain (Figure 1). Mean annual rainfall ranged from 698 mm in the north (Muchea, 1971–2000) to 843 mm in the south (Halls Head, 1971–2000; Australian Bureau of Meteorology 2020) (Figure S1). All species except *B. prionotes* were sampled across the full extent of this rainfall gradient. *Banksia prionotes* was only found across a very narrow (negligible) range (30 mm mean annual rainfall difference) in the sampled study area, but occur more broadly in the region, as do the other study species. The presence (*n* = 19) or absence (*n* = 15) of kangaroos (western grey kangaroo, *Macropus fuliginosus*) as major herbivores was assessed at each site based on sightings of individuals or their scats as well as local knowledge and records (City of Joondalup 2015; City of Nedlands 2014; Ecoscape (Australia Pty Ltd) 2008; Government of Western Australia 2000; Natural Area Consulting 2012). Where present in urban reserves, kangaroos (or signs of their presence) are easily observed, and populations often achieve high density. There was no discernible change in kangaroo abundance over the study period.

#### **2.4 | Field Surveys**

At each site, data were collected on reproductive and size attributes for live individuals. Seedlings less than 1–2 years old in sites older than 4 years since fire (inter-fire seedlings) were excluded as these individuals can have a low survival rate and therefore have little consequence for the reproductive status of populations. Data on the abundance of inter-fire seedlings from the same sites are presented in Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. (2024). Seedlings were distinguished by the presence of cotyledons, lack of signs of current or past reproduction, and were generally <10–20 cm tall for shrub species or <30 cm tall for tree species. Estimates of seedling age were confirmed by observations of seedlings of known age in post-fire sites.

Data were mostly collected within plots positioned to include as many of the target species as possible and ranging in size from 25 to 150 m<sup>2</sup> as necessary to suit different species and plant densities, and to ensure sampling of at least 30 individuals. Plant densities were calculated from the number of individuals in each plot and scaled to the number of plants per hectare. Smaller plots were used for shrub species (density range 0.1–4.6 plants m<sup>−2</sup>), and larger plots for tree species (0.03–1.58 plants m<sup>−2</sup>). At least two plots were established at each site, but where plant density was particularly low, measurements were taken based on a nearest-neighbour search until a minimum of 30 plants were recorded. For some plot-based surveys, additional nearest plants outside of plots were measured to fulfil sample size criterion. Field surveys were undertaken from 2016 to 2018 during peak flowering times for each species (Table 1).

Measurements recorded for each individual included: (1) number of flowers (or inflorescences; all species), (2) number of mature cones with unopened follicles (canopy seed bank species only) and (3) size (all species). *Allocasuarina humilis* is a dioecious species and we identified and recorded attributes of male and female plants separately (only female plants produce cones). The number of cones recorded represents the cumulative canopy seed bank from all previous reproductive seasons excluding seed loss from seed predation, disease and spontaneous follicle opening, among other factors. Size was recorded as aboveground plant height (*Gompholobium tomentosum* and *Acacia pulchella*), canopy volume (*Hibbertia hypericoides* and *Allocasuarina humilis*) or stem diameter at breast height (DBH, 1.37 m above the ground; *Banksia attenuata, B. prionotes*). These measurements were chosen to best represent how size relates to reproductive performance given each species' growth form.

#### **2.5 | Data Analysis**

#### **2.5.1 | Post-Fire Reproductive Trajectories**

To analyse post-fire reproductive trajectories, we evaluated generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) of TSF, herbivory and mean annual rainfall as a priori predictors of each of three population-level reproductive attributes: flowering rate (% individuals flowering), mean number of flowers per plant and mean number of closed cones per plant (for the three serotinous species only). Population-level attributes were calculated from all individuals surveyed, including resprouting and young (nonreproductive) plants, where present. We employed a model selection approach whereby we constructed a set of plausible models from subsets of the a priori predictors and compared these using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc) and AICc model weights (ωAICc) which represent the probability or weight of evidence for each model (Burnham, Anderson, and Huyvaert 2011; Hurvich and Tsai 1989). Models with ΔAICc <5 generally represented a cumulative ωAICc of ≥0.95 and therefore are presented here as part of the 95% confidence set, following Symonds and Moussalli (2011). Models with ΔAICc<2 are considered to have substantial support (Burnham and Anderson 2002). We conducted this analysis in *R* (version 4.0.3) (R Core Team 2020) using the *FSSgam* package (Fisher et al. 2018) which enables an all subsets approach and uses the *gam()* function from the *mgcv* package (Wood 2017).

Flowering rate, presented as proportions, was modelled using a binomial error distribution (logit link function) with data weighted by the number of individuals recorded per site. Mean number of flowers and cones per plant were modelled using a tweedie error distribution (log link function) to account for many zero values (i.e., non-flowering/non-fruiting individuals). TSF was log-transformed for analysis as responses are expected to change most rapidly in the first few years after fire, and to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range. TSF was included as a continuous smoother in the model set to allow for non-linear relationships with time. In all models, the smoothing parameter was limited to a simple spline (k=3) to avoid overfitting. Mean annual rainfall was included as a linear predictor in all models, and any effects were presented as predictions at the 10th and 90th percentile of mean annual rainfall across the TSF chronosequence, representing post-fire reproductive trajectories for 'low' (~720 mm) and 'high' (~790 mm) rainfall sites, respectively.

Herbivory was included as a two-level factor variable (absence or presence of kangaroo herbivores) in model sets for shrub species only (i.e., excluding *B. attenuata* and *B. prionotes*) as we lacked a strong a priori expectation of the effects of herbivory from kangaroos (generally <2 m tall) on tree species that are typically >4 m tall at maturity. A two-way interaction between log-transformed TSF and herbivory was included in the model set for *G. tomentosum* only to explore if effects of herbivory varied by TSF. Replication of different herbivory levels across the range of log-transformed TSF was not considered to be adequate for the other shrub species and therefore was only included as an additive effect in other model sets. An identifier for the year of survey was included as a random smoother in all models for species where measurements were recorded in two successive years to account for repeat measures and any annual variation in environmental conditions (e.g., rainfall) other than an increase in TSF by 1 year.

Modelling of flowering rate and flower counts was conducted separately for male and female plants of the dioecious species *A. humilis*. Top-ranking model comparisons are presented for models on female data only. Only female plants produce cones and seeds and so modelling of cone counts was necessarily restricted to female plant data. Juvenile period was calculated from the flowering rate of female plants. The sex ratio was, on average, 45% females and 55% males across all populations (excluding non-reproductive individuals), or 49% females and 51% males after the post-fire maturation period (i.e., after 4 years) (Figure S2).

#### **2.5.2 | Time Since Fire as a Predictor of Reproduction**

To assess the strength of TSF as a predictor of reproduction, we compared GAMMs with single predictors of either TSF or plant size (height, canopy volume or effective DBH) for each of the three reproductive attributes measured. Models using plant size as the predictor represent the mechanistic relationship between TSF and reproduction, where the growth of plants following fire enables greater access to resources and an increase in reproductive output. For single-cohort populations (i.e., fire-killed species), we would expect that models using single predictors of TSF and plant size would explain similar amounts of variation (i.e., *R*<sup>2</sup>) and have a similar weight of evidence (i.e., AICc and ωAICc). However, for multi-cohort populations (usually resprouters, but also possible for some fire-killed species), we would expect that models using size would explain much more variation and have a much greater weight of evidence than models using TSF.

GAMMs were constructed as outlined above, where models of TSF or size alone were compared using *FSSgam*. Size measurements (height, canopy volume, effective DBH) were log-transformed to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range and improve model fit. For the dioecious species (*A. humilis*), modelling was conducted separately for male and female plants, with top-ranking model comparisons presented for female data only.

the juvenile period for *A. pulchella* by 2.2 years (Table 4). While herbivory was found to impact the flowering rate of *H. hypericoides*, post-fire recovery was so rapid as to not alter the predicted juvenile period (Table 4). High mean annual rainfall increased the juvenile period of *B. attenuata* by 5.7 years (Table 4).

#### **3.2 | Flower and Cone Counts**

TSF consistently appeared in top-ranked models of mean flower count and mean cone count per plant for all species (Table 5). Models suggested that mean flower count increased steadily with increasing TSF for most species except *A. pulchella* (Figure 4). *Acacia pulchella* instead showed a rapid increase in flowering until around 5–8 years post-fire, followed by a slight decline thereafter (Figure 4A). Similarly, female plants of *A. humilis* showed an increase in flowering until around 10–15 years post-fire, followed by a slight decline thereafter (Figure 4B). Male plants of *A. humilis* showed a steady increase in flowering with increasing TSF. The peak mean flower count occurred beyond the predicted minimum tolerable fire interval for all species (Figure 4). At this predicted minimum tolerable fire interval, populations of all species had reached 22%–84% of their peak flower count (Table 3).

Mean annual rainfall appeared in the top-ranked models of mean flower count for the two fire-killed shrub species (*G. tomentosum* and *A. pulchella*) (Table 5). Models predicted that mean flower count was 61% lower in low rainfall sites (10th percentile) compared to high rainfall sites (90th percentile) for these two species across all ages (Figure 5). Herbivory did not appear in any top-ranked models of mean flower count (Table 5).

Populations of *A. humilis* and *B. prionotes* first produced cones 3–4 years post-fire, and mean cone count increased up until 10–15 years post-fire, after which mean cone count was highly variable, with weak evidence of decline in the longer absence of fire (Figure 6). Populations of *B. attenuata* had produced cones even in the youngest sites sampled (1–2 years post-fire), and mean cone count increased steadily with increasing TSF (Figure 6). At the time of their respective predicted minimum tolerable fire intervals, populations of all three serotinous species had reached 45%–91% of their peak cone count (Table 3). Mean annual rainfall did not appear in any top-ranked models for cone counts of these three species (Table 5).

Canopy seed bank density, expressed as the number of cones per hectare, showed a similar although more pronounced nonlinear pattern for *B. prionotes* (Figure S3). On average, seed bank density for *B. prionotes* increased rapidly post-fire up to a maximum of approximately 5500 cones per ha around 10 years and declined thereafter to <1000 cones per ha after 30 years. These seed bank dynamics appear to be driven primarily by changes in plant density (Figure S4), especially a decline in the density of reproductive intermediate-sized trees (2–10 cm DBH) in older sites (Figure S5A), with a minor influence of a decline in reproductive output across various sizes with increasing TSF (Figure S5B).

Canopy seed bank density for *B. attenuata* followed a similar trend to cones per plant, showing an increase from an average of around 500–600 cones per ha in the first five years after fire to an average of around 800–1000 cones per ha in sites older than 20 years (Figure S3). In contrast to *B. prionotes*, seed bank dynamics for the resprouter *B. attenuata* appear to be driven primarily by an increase in individual reproductive output (cones per plant) with increasing TSF (especially in the most productive, largest (>8 cm DBH) trees; Figure S6B), rather than any changes in tree density of this reproductive cohort (Figures S4 and S6A).

#### **3.3 | Time Since Fire Versus Size as a Predictor of Reproduction**

Models using size as a predictor of each of three reproductive attributes were almost always supported by a greater weight of evidence than those using TSF (Table 6). Models of the flowering rate of *A. humilis* showed similar support for size and TSF as the best predictor, although size was still ranked higher than TSF based on AICc (Table 6). This indicates that TSF is not a strong predictor of reproduction in comparison to the underlying mechanistic relationship between size and reproduction. In all but one case (*A. humilis* flowering rate), models using size as a predictor explained greater variation in the data (*R*<sup>2</sup>) than models using TSF (Table 6).

For all species, predicted flowering rate increased rapidly with an increase in size in small plants, with no evidence of a decrease in flowering rate in the largest, and presumably oldest, plants observed (Figure 7). For the tree species, predicted DBH at 50% flowering was 3.3 cm (95% CI [1.9, 5.8]) for *B. attenuata* and 2.9 cm (95% CI [2.5, 3.3]) for *B. prionotes* (Figure 7).

For *A. pulchella*, predicted flower count initially increased with size for plants up to approximately 150 cm tall, but any further increase in size (and presumably age) did not necessarily translate into higher predicted flower counts (Figure 8A).

1	*Australian Journal of Ecology* (1988) **13**, 505-518
2	
3	# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* **L.f. and** *Petrophile pulchella* **(Schrad) R.Br.**
4	
5	R. A. BRADSTOCK\*
6	
7	*School of Biological Sciences. Macleay Building A12, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*
8	
9	M. A. O'CONNELL
10	
11	*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*
12	
13	#### **Abstract**
14	
15	*Plants of* Banksia ericifolia *and* Petrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*
16	
17	*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn fires of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Fires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk of a population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seed-release in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*
18	
19	*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*
20	
21	#### **Introduction**
22	
23	Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).
24	
25	The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fire-prone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia; *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella)* are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles *(B. ericifolia)* or bracts *(P. pulchella).* Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).
26	
27	Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period, Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment post-fire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-
28	
29	\*Present address: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia.
30	
31	
32	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
33	
34	506 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
35	
36	ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).
37	
38	These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning of the vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed fire-management is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.
39	
40	(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?
41	
42	(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?
43	
44	(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?
45	
46	(4) What are the likely trends in numbers and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?
47	
48	(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?
49	
50	#### **Methods**
51	
52	#### *Study sites*
53	
54	The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km.
55	
56	Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.
57	
58	#### *Seedling emergence and survival*
59	
60	The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m<sup>2</sup>) for each species. The number of pre-fire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.
61	
62	The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Burn IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.

68	
69	Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (1 m × 1 m) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.
70	
71	#### *Survival in established plants*
72	
73	Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 m × 1.0 m or 0.5 m × 0.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.
74	
75	Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0-1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.
76	
77	Plants of *P. pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.
78	
79	Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.
80	
81	#### *Seed-survival*
82	
83	Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate of ten cones was harvested 50-100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.
84	
85	Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no effect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of *P. pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.
86	
87	Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.
88	
89	The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. These PV were the differences between the residual and total mean squares expressed as a percentage of the total mean square.

96	#### *Seed-bank estimation*
97	
98	All new cones set in the samples during the study were counted. Cone production during 1984-85 in the 1960 stands was also measured. Collections of 10 cones produced in two flowering seasons between 1981 and 1983 were made from each sample to determine seed-set per cone. A further 10 cones were harvested in areas with only one sample per soil-depth tested. Mean total annual seed production per plant was thus calculated and then described as a function of age by various linear and nonlinear models from which a preferred model was chosen by a comparison of PV.
99	
100	Seed-bank at any given age (per plant) was predicted by estimating the number of seeds (one seed per follicle or bract) set in each of the successive annual cohorts produced up to that age, using the preferred seed production model. In each cohort survival was then calculated using the preferred survival model for each species. The numbers of surviving seeds from each cohort at a given age were then summed to give an estimate of total stored viable seeds for that age. This was repeated for all ages between the time of first reproduction and 40 years. The estimates above 25 years were therefore extrapolations beyond the age limit of the samples. Allowance was made for the time between flowering and fruit maturity which is about one year in both species.
101	
102	A further, alternative estimate of seed-bank was made. Seed production was stopped at age 30 years and the attrition of existing seeds was predicted up to an age of 100 years.
103	
104	#### *Seed-release between fires*
105	
106	The mean number of viable seeds released annually (per plant) in each sample in unburnt conditions was estimated. Samples of cones of four different ages were marked in the 1968 and 1960 samples in mid 1981. Two age classes of cones (1 and 5 years in 1981, method of ageing similar to that described above) were marked in all other samples. The oldest cones in each sample were also marked and in 1981 these were estimated to be 7 and 13 years old. Follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*) which were open and empty were marked. Cones were rechecked after 2 years and the number of follicles/bracts was counted along with those which had opened and shed seeds. Rates of seed-release were compared between samples and cone ages using analysis of variance.
107	
108	All cones set before 1981 were counted in each sample. The mean number of seeds released per plant was then estimated from the product of the measured annual rate of release per cone age class and the mean number of cones in each class. Cones set before 1981 were allocated to the nearest age class and a correction was made for viability.
109	
110	#### *The effect of frequent fires*
111	
112	The effect of three successive fires, separated by intervals of identical length, on the number of plants in a hypothetical stand of each species was estimated. Plants living in the first interval were called first generation and in the second, second generation. The first generation immediate pre-fire number was set at 50 and model stands were assumed to be similar to the sample stands in other respects, such as density. Eleven calculations were done, using values between 5 and 15 years for the 'between-fire' interval.
113	
114	Second generation stand size (*N*) was calculated as a function of the interval (*i*) between fires using:
115	
116	*N* = *B* × *E* × *Ss* × *Se* (1)
117	
118	where *B* = first generation seed-bank size, *E* = proportion of seeds emerging as post-fire seedlings, *Ss* = proportion of seedlings which survive and *Se* = proportion of living plants > 3 years old at *i* years of age. Values of *N* were divided by 50 to give estimates of proportional change in numbers. These estimates were plotted against size of gap between fires. Opposing, extreme values of *E* and *Ss* were used to produce high and low estimates of proportional change.

250	#### **Discussion**
251	
252	#### *Effects of frequent fires*
253	
254	The importance of emergence and survival was reffected in the variability of the interval between fires at which stand replacement would be possible (Fig. 7). Burning at an interval close to 13 years could be done with little regard to other factors such as season or intensity of fire without risk of a decline in numbers. The low levels of emergence and survival (Tables 1,2) used to produce this estimate were the product of a severe drought in the area (Bureau of Meteorology, pers. comm.). It is likely that fires in most years will produce at least a similar or larger number of seedlings. Survival of established plants may also be higher, for this reason.
255	
256	Fire-managers may wish to burn as often as twice a decade, hence it is necessary to know the limit to which fire frequency can be reduced below 13 years without risking a serious decline in numbers. Seasons and intensities of fire may become important in such

265	circumstances as will year to year variability in rainfall.
266	
267	Bradstock (1985) found that emergence in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* varied with rainfall, soil moisture and temperature. High summer temperatures impose a form of exogenous dormancy on seeds (definition of Mott & Groves 1981), restricting emergence to the cooler months. Seeds which lie on the soil over summer lose some viability. The amount of emergence was positively correlated with the period of time the soil surface (0-1.0 cm) remains at field capacity after rain. Seed predation was minimal in burnt areas.
268	
269	Rainfall near the coast in the Sydney Region is highest, on average, from January to July (100-130 mm/month), and lowest from August to December (70-80 mm/month); however, there is great year to year variation.

273	When evaporation is taken into account, the average period of sustained high soil moisture is May-July (early winter). Emergence may therefore be highest after fires which are timed so that most seeds are released in early winter. Seed-release will be most rapid after high intensity fires (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bradstock 1985) and such fires in late summer-autumn will cause most seeds to be released by early winter. In contrast, low inten-

284	sity fires at this time will prolong seed-release over winter and spring. Late summer-autumn, high intensity fires will therefore, on average, yield optimum emergence. A similar fire regime giving optimum emergence in other species of serotinous Proteaceae has been observed by Specht *et al.* (1958), Specht (1981), Bond *et al.* (1984), Cowling and Lamont (1984a, 1984b, 1985), McMahon (1984). Mechanisms in each case were generally similar to those described here.
285	
286	While mortality of plants older than 100 days was due mainly to drought, younger seedlings died during both short dry spells and heavy rain (Bradstock 1985) when they were broken by raindrop impact or washed away. Bradstock (1985) concluded that the risk of death at the most vulnerable age (< 100 days; Table 2) would be minimized when seedlings emerged in early winter. This reinforced the conclusion that late summer fires are optimal in producing seedlings.
287	
288	After successive fires at 8 years, the proportional change in second generation stand size may vary from 9.8 to 0.5 in *B. ericifolia* and from 7.2 to 0.6 in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 7). The daily rainfall patterns for Sydney over 50 years (Bureau of Meterology, pers. comm.) show that a winter containing two successive months of low soil surface moisture occurs on average once every decade whereas very wet winters in which the soil is more or less continually moist occur several times a decade (Bradstock 1985). Thus fires of optimal season and intensity occurring 8 years apart would be followed by a dry winter and a subsequent decline in post-fire numbers, once every 80-100 years. More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years. A 6-8 year cycle would be hazardous, due to a lower seed-bank and the increased probability of encountering dry post-fire conditions.
289	
290	Reproduction is delayed in *B. ericifolia* growing on shallow soils and such stands may decline when fires occur less than 15 years apart. Observations indicate that the primary juvenile period may extend to more than 8 years and also that the seed-bank size may be less than on deep soils.
291	
292	There are, therefore, two consecutive phases in which plants are susceptible to recurrent fires: first, during the primary juvenile period and second, the subsequent time up to the age at which exact self-replacement of stands is possible. So far most attention has been given to describing the lengths of primary juvenile periods. Values given here fell within the ranges already reported for these species (Benson 1985) and for other serotinous obligate seeders of the Proteaceae (3-11 years; Kruger 1983; Lamont 1985). Measurements of this second critical phase need to be made if serotinous obligate seeders are to be used as indicator species in fire-prone vegetation. It
293

295

297	
298	may be useful if correlations exist between this and other demographic characteristics, particularly the length of the primary juvenile period. For example, is first reproduction at an early age always followed by a short interval to the age of self-replacement or vice versa?
299	
300	Replacement ages for the study species were similar, despite differences in seedling-survival, early rates of development of seed-bank and primary juvenile period. Gill and McMahon (1986) reported that in *Banksia ornata*, a serotinous obligate seeder, common in parts of southern Australia, stand replacement may be likely after 16 years of age if post-fire emergence took place from 20% of available seeds. Seeds first become available at about 6 years in *B. ornata* (Gill & McMahon 1986), a figure comparable to that in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella.* Despite this similarity, populations of *B. ornata* may decline under some repeated cycles of fire less than 15 years apart, whilst *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* populations may increase or remain stable. This difference was primarily due to a slower rate of accumulation of seed-bank in *B. ornata*, though other possible differences in projected survival rate were also present. Similarly, Kruger and Bigalke (1984) reported that in *Protea repens,* a shrub of the South African fynbos, the primary juvenile period may be 4-5 years (ripe seeds first available), but replacement age may be 10-12 years. It is most prudent to conclude that there is little current evidence of any consistent linkage between these key events. Further demographic studies amongst a wider range of species are needed to confirm this.
301	
302	#### *Effects of infrequent fires*
303	
304	The present study was hampered by a lack of old populations (>25 years). This prevented direct measurements of life span and seed-production in very old plants. It was necessary to extrapolate trends from younger populations and anecdotal evidence to describe what happens when fire is excluded for long periods.
305	
306	In the seed-bank models (Fig. 5) seed-production was arbitrarily set to cease at 30 years. However, Bradstock and Myerscough (1981) observed the occurrence of stands of *B. ericifolia* older than this (these also contained *P. pulchella*) in which seeds were still being produced. The modeled storages will therefore underestimate the trend in real stands. Nevertheless, these suggested that enough seeds would be available for replacement for up to about 45 years in *B. ericifolia* and 90 years in *P. pulchella.* The life spans of these species are more likely to be less than 50 years (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981), hence in reality, senescence will hasten the decline of the seed-bank through the death of plants and replacement ages may be much nearer 30 years. The fall of viable seeds onto the litter and soil will increase as a consequence and, if seed-production occurs beyond 30 years, this pool of released seeds will be very large. If these assumptions are correct, changes in number and seed-bank may be quite similar in their pattern to those described by Gill and McMahon 1986 for *B. ornata.* Kruger and Bigalke (1984) also reported a similar decline in numbers after 30 years in some serotinous obligate seeders from South African shrublands, and suggested that life spans for dominant species of this kind fell within the range 20-50 years.
307	
308	In samples that are more than 20 years of age the number of viable seeds released each year (Fig. 6) greatly exceeded the number of plants that died annually (Figs 1, 2). Bradstock (1985) found that the heavy cover of plants and seedling predators restricted establishment from this pool of available seeds. However, a few seedlings are likely to survive in both species. A rough calculation can be done to estimate the number which may establish in a stand of 50 plants. Average conditions of soil moisture in any year will usually be adequate to give 10% emergence of available seeds. If 5% of these survive for 3 years (about eight times lower survival than in burnt conditions; Table 2), then 21-24 year old stands would produce two (*B. ericifolia*) and 12 (*P. pulchella*) seedlings annually. Such recruits would join the ranks of small suppressed plants which are subject to high mortality and would probably have little chance of reproducing (Bradstock 1985).
309	
310	At greater ages, when seed-release and mortality may be high, gaps in the canopy caused by senescence of dominants may appear. Seedling predators may become satiated as a result (e.g. Bond 1984a; O'Dowd & Gill 1984) and these conditions may promote the emergence, growth and reproduction of new plants. The relative abilities of *B. ericifolia, P. pulchella*
311	
312	
313	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
314	
315	516 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
316	
317	and other species to exploit gaps and openings may determine whether self-perpetuation in large numbers is possible in the absence of fire. More work is needed to determine regeneration processes in older stands and their scarcity means that some effort needs to be made to preserve unburnt areas in the future.
318	
319	Fires, 20-30 years apart, will create very high density stands and the absence of these in the study area may be due to a history of burning at a higher frequency.
320	
321	#### *Effects of density*
322	
323	Fire regimes may be used to increase or decrease the density of stands. For instance, if the relationships in Figs 1-7 hold true for much of the potential range of densities, then it may be possible, for example, to thin very dense stands and then hold them in this state. Several adverse fire-cycles (e.g. low intensity spring fires, less than 10 years apart) followed by a 10 year cycle of high intensity autumn fires would achieve this result.
324	
325	The density of a stand will change with age as plants die and the chronosequence in Table 3 may indicate the approximate trend. Bradstock (1985) found that density had no effect on the survival of seedlings older than 100 days. There were also no obvious effects of density on survival at older ages in either species, including the 1975 samples in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 2; Table 3), although dead plants tended to be small suppressed individuals in both species. Morris and Myerscough (1983, 1988) found evidence for density-dependent mortality in *B. ericifolia* stands of very high density (initial sample: 140 plants m<sup>-2</sup>) between the ages of 4 and 9 years.
326	
327	In both *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella,* the proportion of plants that continues to produce cones declined with age (Bradstock 1985) so that over time the increase in reproductive effort (Fig. 4) came from a small number of dominant individuals (Bradstock 1985). This pattern of reproduction amongst individuals may affect the relationship between density and seed-bank if the survival of dominant reproductive plants is unaffected by the number of suppressed individuals. The number of plants which reproduce and the amount of seeds produced may then be fixed above a moderate threshold of density, as indicated by experimental studies in other single-species populations (Harper 1977; Silvertown 1982). Further evidence of Morris and Myerscough (1988) showed that *B. ericifolia* plants at densities of 27.5 plants m<sup>-2</sup> had set a mean of 345 ± 92 seeds m<sup>-2</sup> at 8 years whereas high density plants (142 m<sup>-2</sup>) produced 225 ± 80 seeds m<sup>-2</sup>. If seed-bank size is fixed across the upper range of densities then its prime determinant will be stand age. The perpetuation of very dense stands would then be possible only after longer fire-free intervals than those described here for lower density samples.
328	
329	Density and numbers may also be influenced by pollinators. Paton and Turner (1985) found that introduced bees may double the numbers of seeds set in *B. ericifolia* cones. The introduction of exotic bees may therefore have caused a massive increase in density and numbers in stands containing this species without any concurrent change in fire frequency. Other changes in species composition may have followed.
330	
331	#### **Conclusions**
332	
333	All components of fire regime can influence a change in numbers and density, between generations, of *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella.* However, the largest change was due to differences in the age at which stands were burnt and the proportion of seeds which emerged as seedlings. Seasonal controls on seedling establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods, effects of seed or seedling predators in unburnt conditions, and changes in structure of old stands and life spans, are generally similar in southern hemisphere species, particularly within the family, Proteaceae. However, demographic behaviour of fire-prone species cannot be predicted solely from any single characteristic such as survival, degree of serotiny (seed-survival in cones), seed-bank size or success of emergence. Any attempt to compare and classify species on their relative ability to withstand specific fire regimes, without a quantitative overview of the life-cycle, could be misleading.
334	
335	There may be little reason to assume that if reproduction commences early, then enough seeds will also be available to ensure replacement at a relatively early age. Quantitative variations in all the important components of the
336	
337	
338	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
339	
340	*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 517
341	
342	life-cycle may exist within a species and correlations between these components and obvious site factors need to be studied (e.g. Cowling & Lamont 1985). Managers concerned with conserving populations at stable numbers should therefore use, as an indicator of the minimum interval between fires, the serotinous obligate seeder within their estate, that is slowest to reach self-replacement.

*Australian Journal of Ecology* (1988) **13**, 505-518

# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* **L.f. and** *Petrophile pulchella* **(Schrad) R.Br.**

R. A. BRADSTOCK\*

*School of Biological Sciences. Macleay Building A12, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*

M. A. O'CONNELL

*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*

#### **Abstract**

*Plants of* Banksia ericifolia *and* Petrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*

*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn fires of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Fires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk of a population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seed-release in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*

*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*

#### **Introduction**

Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).

The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fire-prone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia; *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella)* are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles *(B. ericifolia)* or bracts *(P. pulchella).* Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).

Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period, Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment post-fire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-

\*Present address: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia.


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

506 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).

These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning of the vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed fire-management is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.

(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?

(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?

(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?

(4) What are the likely trends in numbers and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?

(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?

#### **Methods**

#### *Study sites*

The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km.

Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.

#### *Seedling emergence and survival*

The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m<sup>2</sup>) for each species. The number of pre-fire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.

The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Burn IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 507

Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (1 m × 1 m) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.

#### *Survival in established plants*

Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 m × 1.0 m or 0.5 m × 0.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.

Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0-1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.

Plants of *P. pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.

Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.

#### *Seed-survival*

Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate of ten cones was harvested 50-100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.

Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no effect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of *P. pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.

Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.

The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. These PV were the differences between the residual and total mean squares expressed as a percentage of the total mean square.


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

508 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

#### *Seed-bank estimation*

All new cones set in the samples during the study were counted. Cone production during 1984-85 in the 1960 stands was also measured. Collections of 10 cones produced in two flowering seasons between 1981 and 1983 were made from each sample to determine seed-set per cone. A further 10 cones were harvested in areas with only one sample per soil-depth tested. Mean total annual seed production per plant was thus calculated and then described as a function of age by various linear and nonlinear models from which a preferred model was chosen by a comparison of PV.

Seed-bank at any given age (per plant) was predicted by estimating the number of seeds (one seed per follicle or bract) set in each of the successive annual cohorts produced up to that age, using the preferred seed production model. In each cohort survival was then calculated using the preferred survival model for each species. The numbers of surviving seeds from each cohort at a given age were then summed to give an estimate of total stored viable seeds for that age. This was repeated for all ages between the time of first reproduction and 40 years. The estimates above 25 years were therefore extrapolations beyond the age limit of the samples. Allowance was made for the time between flowering and fruit maturity which is about one year in both species.

A further, alternative estimate of seed-bank was made. Seed production was stopped at age 30 years and the attrition of existing seeds was predicted up to an age of 100 years.

#### *Seed-release between fires*

The mean number of viable seeds released annually (per plant) in each sample in unburnt conditions was estimated. Samples of cones of four different ages were marked in the 1968 and 1960 samples in mid 1981. Two age classes of cones (1 and 5 years in 1981, method of ageing similar to that described above) were marked in all other samples. The oldest cones in each sample were also marked and in 1981 these were estimated to be 7 and 13 years old. Follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*) which were open and empty were marked. Cones were rechecked after 2 years and the number of follicles/bracts was counted along with those which had opened and shed seeds. Rates of seed-release were compared between samples and cone ages using analysis of variance.

All cones set before 1981 were counted in each sample. The mean number of seeds released per plant was then estimated from the product of the measured annual rate of release per cone age class and the mean number of cones in each class. Cones set before 1981 were allocated to the nearest age class and a correction was made for viability.

#### *The effect of frequent fires*

The effect of three successive fires, separated by intervals of identical length, on the number of plants in a hypothetical stand of each species was estimated. Plants living in the first interval were called first generation and in the second, second generation. The first generation immediate pre-fire number was set at 50 and model stands were assumed to be similar to the sample stands in other respects, such as density. Eleven calculations were done, using values between 5 and 15 years for the 'between-fire' interval.

Second generation stand size (*N*) was calculated as a function of the interval (*i*) between fires using:

*N* = *B* × *E* × *Ss* × *Se* (1)

where *B* = first generation seed-bank size, *E* = proportion of seeds emerging as post-fire seedlings, *Ss* = proportion of seedlings which survive and *Se* = proportion of living plants > 3 years old at *i* years of age. Values of *N* were divided by 50 to give estimates of proportional change in numbers. These estimates were plotted against size of gap between fires. Opposing, extreme values of *E* and *Ss* were used to produce high and low estimates of proportional change.

#### **Results**

#### *Seedling emergence and survival*

In both species, emergence was spread over periods of up to 9 months after the fires or experiments. The number, density and proportion of seedlings that emerged from seeds were variable (Table 1). Pulses of emergence pro-


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 509

duced cohorts with differing birth dates in each natural fire. In *B. ericifolia* the power and exponential models were found to be the models of best fit (Table 2) while in *P. pulchella* the power function was the model of best fit (Table 2). In some cases neither model fitted the data well (Table 2).

#### *Survival in established plants*

*Banksia ericifolia:* Sample densities are given in Table 3. No significant difference in the overall proportion of deaths was found between samples (P>0.10), on shallow soils. There were too few deaths to allow comparison

#### **Discussion**

#### *Effects of frequent fires*

The importance of emergence and survival was reffected in the variability of the interval between fires at which stand replacement would be possible (Fig. 7). Burning at an interval close to 13 years could be done with little regard to other factors such as season or intensity of fire without risk of a decline in numbers. The low levels of emergence and survival (Tables 1,2) used to produce this estimate were the product of a severe drought in the area (Bureau of Meteorology, pers. comm.). It is likely that fires in most years will produce at least a similar or larger number of seedlings. Survival of established plants may also be higher, for this reason.

Fire-managers may wish to burn as often as twice a decade, hence it is necessary to know the limit to which fire frequency can be reduced below 13 years without risking a serious decline in numbers. Seasons and intensities of fire may become important in such

circumstances as will year to year variability in rainfall.

Bradstock (1985) found that emergence in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* varied with rainfall, soil moisture and temperature. High summer temperatures impose a form of exogenous dormancy on seeds (definition of Mott & Groves 1981), restricting emergence to the cooler months. Seeds which lie on the soil over summer lose some viability. The amount of emergence was positively correlated with the period of time the soil surface (0-1.0 cm) remains at field capacity after rain. Seed predation was minimal in burnt areas.

Rainfall near the coast in the Sydney Region is highest, on average, from January to July (100-130 mm/month), and lowest from August to December (70-80 mm/month); however, there is great year to year variation.

FIG. 5. Mean number of stored viable seeds (seed-bank) per plant, under two regimes of seed production: continuous (——), ceased at 30 years (- - -).

When evaporation is taken into account, the average period of sustained high soil moisture is May-July (early winter). Emergence may therefore be highest after fires which are timed so that most seeds are released in early winter. Seed-release will be most rapid after high intensity fires (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bradstock 1985) and such fires in late summer-autumn will cause most seeds to be released by early winter. In contrast, low inten-

sity fires at this time will prolong seed-release over winter and spring. Late summer-autumn, high intensity fires will therefore, on average, yield optimum emergence. A similar fire regime giving optimum emergence in other species of serotinous Proteaceae has been observed by Specht *et al.* (1958), Specht (1981), Bond *et al.* (1984), Cowling and Lamont (1984a, 1984b, 1985), McMahon (1984). Mechanisms in each case were generally similar to those described here.

While mortality of plants older than 100 days was due mainly to drought, younger seedlings died during both short dry spells and heavy rain (Bradstock 1985) when they were broken by raindrop impact or washed away. Bradstock (1985) concluded that the risk of death at the most vulnerable age (< 100 days; Table 2) would be minimized when seedlings emerged in early winter. This reinforced the conclusion that late summer fires are optimal in producing seedlings.

After successive fires at 8 years, the proportional change in second generation stand size may vary from 9.8 to 0.5 in *B. ericifolia* and from 7.2 to 0.6 in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 7). The daily rainfall patterns for Sydney over 50 years (Bureau of Meterology, pers. comm.) show that a winter containing two successive months of low soil surface moisture occurs on average once every decade whereas very wet winters in which the soil is more or less continually moist occur several times a decade (Bradstock 1985). Thus fires of optimal season and intensity occurring 8 years apart would be followed by a dry winter and a subsequent decline in post-fire numbers, once every 80-100 years. More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years. A 6-8 year cycle would be hazardous, due to a lower seed-bank and the increased probability of encountering dry post-fire conditions.

Reproduction is delayed in *B. ericifolia* growing on shallow soils and such stands may decline when fires occur less than 15 years apart. Observations indicate that the primary juvenile period may extend to more than 8 years and also that the seed-bank size may be less than on deep soils.

There are, therefore, two consecutive phases in which plants are susceptible to recurrent fires: first, during the primary juvenile period and second, the subsequent time up to the age at which exact self-replacement of stands is possible. So far most attention has been given to describing the lengths of primary juvenile periods. Values given here fell within the ranges already reported for these species (Benson 1985) and for other serotinous obligate seeders of the Proteaceae (3-11 years; Kruger 1983; Lamont 1985). Measurements of this second critical phase need to be made if serotinous obligate seeders are to be used as indicator species in fire-prone vegetation. It

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 515

may be useful if correlations exist between this and other demographic characteristics, particularly the length of the primary juvenile period. For example, is first reproduction at an early age always followed by a short interval to the age of self-replacement or vice versa?

Replacement ages for the study species were similar, despite differences in seedling-survival, early rates of development of seed-bank and primary juvenile period. Gill and McMahon (1986) reported that in *Banksia ornata*, a serotinous obligate seeder, common in parts of southern Australia, stand replacement may be likely after 16 years of age if post-fire emergence took place from 20% of available seeds. Seeds first become available at about 6 years in *B. ornata* (Gill & McMahon 1986), a figure comparable to that in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella.* Despite this similarity, populations of *B. ornata* may decline under some repeated cycles of fire less than 15 years apart, whilst *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* populations may increase or remain stable. This difference was primarily due to a slower rate of accumulation of seed-bank in *B. ornata*, though other possible differences in projected survival rate were also present. Similarly, Kruger and Bigalke (1984) reported that in *Protea repens,* a shrub of the South African fynbos, the primary juvenile period may be 4-5 years (ripe seeds first available), but replacement age may be 10-12 years. It is most prudent to conclude that there is little current evidence of any consistent linkage between these key events. Further demographic studies amongst a wider range of species are needed to confirm this.

#### *Effects of infrequent fires*

The present study was hampered by a lack of old populations (>25 years). This prevented direct measurements of life span and seed-production in very old plants. It was necessary to extrapolate trends from younger populations and anecdotal evidence to describe what happens when fire is excluded for long periods.

In the seed-bank models (Fig. 5) seed-production was arbitrarily set to cease at 30 years. However, Bradstock and Myerscough (1981) observed the occurrence of stands of *B. ericifolia* older than this (these also contained *P. pulchella*) in which seeds were still being produced. The modeled storages will therefore underestimate the trend in real stands. Nevertheless, these suggested that enough seeds would be available for replacement for up to about 45 years in *B. ericifolia* and 90 years in *P. pulchella.* The life spans of these species are more likely to be less than 50 years (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981), hence in reality, senescence will hasten the decline of the seed-bank through the death of plants and replacement ages may be much nearer 30 years. The fall of viable seeds onto the litter and soil will increase as a consequence and, if seed-production occurs beyond 30 years, this pool of released seeds will be very large. If these assumptions are correct, changes in number and seed-bank may be quite similar in their pattern to those described by Gill and McMahon 1986 for *B. ornata.* Kruger and Bigalke (1984) also reported a similar decline in numbers after 30 years in some serotinous obligate seeders from South African shrublands, and suggested that life spans for dominant species of this kind fell within the range 20-50 years.

In samples that are more than 20 years of age the number of viable seeds released each year (Fig. 6) greatly exceeded the number of plants that died annually (Figs 1, 2). Bradstock (1985) found that the heavy cover of plants and seedling predators restricted establishment from this pool of available seeds. However, a few seedlings are likely to survive in both species. A rough calculation can be done to estimate the number which may establish in a stand of 50 plants. Average conditions of soil moisture in any year will usually be adequate to give 10% emergence of available seeds. If 5% of these survive for 3 years (about eight times lower survival than in burnt conditions; Table 2), then 21-24 year old stands would produce two (*B. ericifolia*) and 12 (*P. pulchella*) seedlings annually. Such recruits would join the ranks of small suppressed plants which are subject to high mortality and would probably have little chance of reproducing (Bradstock 1985).

At greater ages, when seed-release and mortality may be high, gaps in the canopy caused by senescence of dominants may appear. Seedling predators may become satiated as a result (e.g. Bond 1984a; O'Dowd & Gill 1984) and these conditions may promote the emergence, growth and reproduction of new plants. The relative abilities of *B. ericifolia, P. pulchella*
